replying_to: Replying to Fishr: Invariant Gradient Variances for Out-of-distribution Generalization
display_title: Official Review of Paper107 by Reviewer KDTu

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new regularization method for OOD generalization. The central idea is to align the covariances of gradients between different domains. Specifically,
- Authors first categorize different works in this area into three groups:
    1. Methods that match **features** across domains such as those in adversarial training and most notably CORAL which considers the covariance of the **features**.
    2. Methods that state that **the classifier on the top** should be invariant. Such as IRM.
    3. Those that align **gradients** such as IGA.

- Authors then propose Fishr which falls into the 3rd category. It aligns gradients between the domain but with the important different that it aligns the *covariance* of the gradients not the *average* of them.

- Authors establish equivalences between the the covariance, the fisher information matrix, and the hessian which in fact describes the loss landscape.

- As a practical approach, authors propose to match the **variances** instead of the **covariances** and also only the penultimate linear layer.

- Finally, authors evaluate their approach on standard OOD benchmarks in two different setups:
    1. When the hyper-parameters are tuned using the test set.
    2. When the hyper-parameters are tuned using the training set.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The paper does a very good job at explaining the previous work in a coherent way.
- The idea of matching the covariances of gradients is neat and well-motivated. Although hand wavy at points, but I enjoyed the connection to the loss landscape and the fisher.
- The paper is **almost** well-written with some comments that I provide below.
- I also found Figures 3-6 that visualize the dynamics intuitive.

Weaknesses:
- The paper first motivates that use of the covariance matrix but in the end, it uses a crude approximation of the method. The covariance matrix is approximated by the its diagonal (so variance not covariance). Also the method is only applied on the last layer.
    - That being said, I understand that using the covariance matrix is impractical and I believe that penalizing the last layer only might be even a must not just an approximation (I outline below).
- I have a hard time justifying myself, why the covariances must match. The distributions of the training domains **are** in fact different. As an example, in a dataset like PACS, I do not believe that the covariances of real images and sketch images should be matched. So it appears that authors are making an implicit assumption about the similarity of different training domains. However, I understand that it is an assumption being extensively used in this literature and is a step towards relaxing the IID assumption.
- So, as I said, I believe that it might not make sense to match the covariances. However, thanks to your approximation (that the method is only applied to the last layer), matching the variances at the last layer, might still allow the network to have drastically different distributions in earlier layers. This is both good and bad. Good because it relaxes the assumption that all the domains should match. Bad because it defeats your motivation to some extent.
- With that perspective, your method appears as a better approximation of IRM to me. Because it is only applied to the last layer, so making sure that the last layer is shared between the domains. Yet, it allows for the earlier layers to have domain-specific features.
- The main weakness of this paper is the empirical results in my opinion. When the model selection is by using the training domain, all the methods are statistically the same. Even with the test set is used for model selection, Fishr does not perform very well.

A comment regarding the writing:
- The actual experimental results comes very late in the paper. I suggest swapping sections 4 and 5.

Minor comments:
- If the citations are in a different color, it would be easier to read.
- In page 1, I am not sure what does the word "feedback" refer to.
- Just before Eq. 1, use \cite not \citep for "(Koyama & ..."
- I suggest rewriting the last sentence on page 3. 
- A dot is missing at the end of Eq. 2.
- I suggest rewriting the sentence right after Eq. 4.
- In the caption of the tables, mention what bold number and underlined number mean.
content.summary_of_the_review:
As mentioned above, in summary,

(+) The central idea of the paper is interesting.\
(+) The paper is rather well-written with very good related work section.\
(-) The practical implementation is a crude approximation of the central idea.\
(+) The colored-mnist experiments confirms the underlying intuition.\
(-) Other empirical results are very poor (in my opinion).

My questions:
- I would like to know if the authors agree with me that only applying Fishr to the last layer might in fact be a necessity when the training domain are much more different. For example, when one domain is an mnist with 10 classes and another is an mnist with 5 classes.
- I appreciate if the authors could comment on why not matching the **uncentered covariances**, i.e., matching the mean as well as the variance.
- What would happen if you train your method for much more epochs (like 5000 epoch on the colored-mnist)? Most the OOD methods fall back to ERM in the long run because the penalty is zero even for ERM at the convergence. I am curious to see what would happen to Fishr.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper107 by Reviewer KDTu

content.title: Response to reviewer KDTu (1/3)
content.comment:
Dear reviewer KDTu, we thank you for your deep understanding of the paper, for highlighting its strengths and weaknesses - that we have tried to solve in our latest revision.
We will answer your questions below.

**Comment1**: Fishr is a better approximation of IRM

**Response1**: To empirically check this idea, we have tried to match the gradient variances only in the features extractor - while ignoring the gradients in the classifier. This further improves accuracy on Colored MNIST (from 69.5 to 73.8). In other words, we managed to reduce domain shifts without explicitly forcing the predictors to be simultaneously optimal. This shows that Fishr is not just a better approximation of the IRM condition.
Moreover, we also applied the Fishr regularization in all layers: *i.e.*, in the features extractor and in the classifier simultaneously. This obtains the best trade-off between train and test accuracies.
These results, now included in Table 2, can be reproduced by calling https://anonymous.4open.science/r/fishr-anonymous-EBB6/coloredmnist/train_coloredmnist.py.
This also shows that applying the gradient variance matching only on the last layer is not always a necessity.

**Comment2**: Applying Fishr to the last layer might in fact be a necessity when the training domains are much more different. For example, when one domain is an mnist with 10 classes and another is an mnist with 5 classes.

**Response2**:
We agree with you: we also think this approximation improves performances if domains are very different, notably to tackle what [1] named “diversity shifts”, when “each domain represents a certain spectrum of diversity in data”. In this case, the features extractor needs to have domain-variant low-level layers, to handle differences in pixel distributions and extract “domain-specific features” as stated. This was notably argued in Appendix C.2.2, where we showed that IGA on the full network works badly on PACS: IGA benefited from being applied only in the last layer (Table 12). 

This holds true for all real-world datasets from DomainBed, and also for the modified Colored MNIST you suggested, where the first domain has 10 digits and the second has only 5 digits. We verified this empirically by keeping only digits {0,1,2,5,6} in the domain 80% from Colored MNIST in the IRM setup. Note that the dataset still has a binary label corresponding to {<5, >=5}. Results are reported in the following table.

| Method              | Train acc. | Test acc. | Test acc. in {0,1,2,5,6} | Test acc. in {3,4,7,8,9} |
|---------------------|------------|-----------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| ERM                 | 88.5       | 14.2      | 17.5                     | 11.4                     |
| IRM                 | 82.6       | 31.3      | 52.2                     | 12.5                     |
| Fishr in all layers | 80.5       | 40.4      | 56.8                     | 24.7                     |
| Fishr in classifier | 72.9       | 57.5      | 72.1                     | 43.7                     |
| Fishr in extractor  | 81.7       | 36.3      | 53.7                     | 20.0                     |

This confirms previous insights: Fishr applied only in the last layer works better than in the full network (even though still performing better than IRM). Notably, Fishr in the last layer performs well (72.1%) on digits {0,1,2,5,6} for which the color was explicitly a spurious feature. The lack of “generalization transferability” to digits {3,4,7,8,9} is a promising question for future works. 

In addition, this last-layer approximation is often necessary for computational reasons: for example in DomainBed, computing the domain-level gradient variances for all weights in a ResNet-50 could not fit in the memory of our GPUs. Yet, as shown in our previous answer, it’s worth noting that the more expensive Fishr on all layers may work better when tackling only correlation shifts [1] as in Colored MNIST, where “the correlation relationship flips across the environments”.

(End of the response in the next comment)

content.title: Response to reviewer KDTu (2/3)
content.comment:
**End of response2**: Finally, we also tried a new “label shift” experiment that we suspect may interest reviewer KDTu (even more so if it’s the experiment the reviewer has suggested). The setup is similar to previously, except that this is now a classification with 10 classes (the 10 digits from 0 to 9). In other words, domain 80% only has samples from 5 labels (0,1,2,5,6) out of 10. The challenge is quite different: while we previously tackle diversity shifts (the two labels {<5, >=5} are in Domain 80%, yet not in their full “multimodalities”), we now tackle label shifts (the labels {3,4,7,8,9} are not in Domain 80%.).

| Method              | Train acc. | Test acc. | Test acc. in {0,1,2,5,6} | Test acc. in {3,4,7,8,9} | Train acc. | Test acc. | Test acc. in {0,1,2,5,6} | Test acc. in {3,4,7,8,9} |
|---------------------|------------|-----------|--------------------------|--------------------------|------------|-----------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| Class conditional   | ✗    | ✗   | ✗                  | ✗                  | ✓    | ✓   | ✓                  | ✓                  |
| ERM                 | 85.0       | 13.4      | 17.9                     | 9.1                      | N/A        | N/A       | N/A                      | N/A                      |
| IRM                 | 81.8       | 17.9      | 27.8                     | 8.5                      | 78.0       | 33.3      | 58.7                     | 9.2                      |
| Fishr in all layers | 80.5       | 28.3      | 48.1                     | 8.9                      | 68.0       | 39.3      | 72.5                     | 7.3                      |
| Fishr in classifier | 80.0       | 28.4      | 48.4                     | 9.0                      | 74.2       | 40.2      | 67.6                     | 13.5                     |
| Fishr in extractor | 81.2       | 25.8      | 43.7                     | 8.9                      |  65.3     | 39.9     | 76.7                    |  4.1                   |

In that case, all approaches fail badly, even Fishr applied on the last layer. 
Yet, this can be fixed (at least partially) by class-conditioning as in CDANN [2]: for Fishr, we compute gradient variances per class, and then match only the class-conditioned gradient variances for the five classes shared across the two domains. This improves accuracy for classes {0,1,2,5,6}. Yet, accuracies remain low for the five other untackled classes.

[1] Ye, Nanyang, et al. "OoD-Bench: Benchmarking and Understanding Out-of-Distribution Generalization Datasets and Algorithms." arXiv (2021).

[2] Li, Ya, et al. "Domain generalization via conditional invariant representations." AAAI. 2018.

**Comment3**: Why not match the uncentered covariances ?

**Response3**: As previously discussed in Appendix B.2.5, we have also tried to match uncentered variances. It was a promising lead because it would theoretically strengthen the connection between Fishr and the Hessian, as the uncentered gradient variance is proportional to the empirical Fisher Information matrix. Second, this would implicitly incorporate the mean-gradient matching (motivated in IGA/Fish) inside Fishr. Yet, in practice, we have not noticed any significant difference, as reported in Table 6 on Colored MNIST. This was empirically confirmed in DomainBed: for example, Fishr with either centered or uncentered variances reach 67.8 in ‘Oracle’ OfficeHome. As *the two approaches perform closely*, by similarity with CORAL and to further differentiate Fishr from IGA/Fish, we chose to match the centered variances.

Yet, it’s worth noting that explicitly matching simultaneously the gradient centered variances (Fishr) along with the gradient means (IGA) performs best in Appendix C.2.2, on Colored MNIST and OfficeHome. This is at the cost of one additional hyperparameter: the regularization strength for the gradient mean matching. Overall, these questions are promising for future works that would consider the complementarity of these gradient-based methods, or introduce new (adversarial?) strategies to align gradient distributions.

content.title: Response to reviewer KDTu (3/3)
content.comment:
**Comment4**: Train your method for much more epochs

**Response4**: Increasing the number of training epochs from 501 to 5000 provides the following results:

| Method                                      | Train acc. | Test acc. | Train acc. | Test acc. | Train acc. | Test acc. |
|---------------------------------------------|------------|-----------|------------|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Training steps                              | 501        | 501       | 5000       | 5000      | 5000       | 5000      |
| Linear increase in $\lambda$ after step 500 | N/A        | N/A       | ✗    | ✗   | ✓    | ✓   |
| ERM                                         | 86.4       | 14.0      | 95.2       | 23.6      | N/A        | N/A       |
| IRM                                         | 71.0       | 65.6      | 75.7       | 60.4      | 74.8       | 62.2      |
| V-REx                                       | 71.7       | 67.2      | 75.4       | 64.8      | 73.5       | 67.7      |
| Fishr in all layers                         | 69.6       | 71.2      | 72.7       | 66.9      | 70.0       | 68.7      |
| Fishr in classifier                    | 71.0       | 69.5      | 74.4       | 65.2      | 71.8       | 69.5      |
| Fishr in extractor                    | 65.6 | 73.8 | 71.8     | 67.1     | 66.9      | 70.5     |  

So the ranking in test accuracy is consistent across methods, yet results tend to get closer with additional training steps.
Pushing to 100k training steps, we indeed observe that Fishr collapses slowly to ERM. More generally, we confirm that for all methods (even ERM), the Fishr penalty tends towards zero after sufficient steps. Yet, this is not by learning invariance across domains, but merely because as the network perfectly predicts all training samples, the training gradients tend towards zero, and thus so do gradient variances and the Fishr penalty. Thus for Fishr, because the regularization’s impact declines little by little, the network eventually learns the color shortcut as it naturally does without regularization.

To fix this behavior, a simple solution is to gradually increase the regularization strength hyperparameter $\lambda$. When the increase is linear after step 500, all methods become less sensitive to the number of training epochs. Another solution specific for Fishr would be to normalize the gradient norms, for example by maximizing the cosine similarity across variances rather than minimizing their euclidean distances.

Finally, please read our responses to other reviewers regarding the empirical significance of our approach.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper107 by Reviewer ZMd5

content.title: Response to reviewer ZMd5 (1/2)
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer ZMd5. Thank you for your comments.

**Comment1**: The proposed method is based on intuition and directly inherits from the previous methods, which I think is quite ad-hoc. There is no theoretical analysis to support the regularization, for example, why it is necessary to incorporate the covariance, which setting can it solve, etc

**Response1**: We introduce a new regularization to enforce invariance across different training domains in which there is a constant underlying causal mechanism. This follows the standard assumption from [1], as stated in the second paragraph of the introduction. This aims at tackling the distribution shifts across those training domains, which are usually diversity shifts and correlation shifts - as defined in the first paragraph of the “Context and related work” Section.

To make our paper appealing and understandable, we first provide intuitions, always backed up by previous papers (notably in Section 3.2). Then Section 3.3 is a rich and consistent theoretical analysis of Fishr. That’s why we firmly disagree with your statement: “There is no theoretical analysis to support the regularization”. In contrast, we justify Fishr with the theoretical relations between the gradient covariance, the Fisher Information and the Hessian of the objective. We also theoretically prove that Fishr leads to reduced domain inconsistencies in Appendix A.1. 

Moreover, it’s not “necessary” to incorporate the covariance: yet, we show theoretically and empirically that it’s sufficient to match Hessians across domains (see Table 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 6), while being much more efficient than alternatives (such as AND-mask, which fails on DomainBed). Fishr is also sufficient to match domain risks (see Fig. 4 introduced in Section 3.2). Please see our response to the first comment of Reviewer iWJv for more differences between Fishr and previous methods, in particular Fish.

[1] Blanchard, Gilles, Gyemin Lee, and Clayton Scott. "Generalizing from several related classification tasks to a new unlabeled sample." NeurIPS (2011).

**Comment2**: The experimental results are not good enough to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Firstly, why using the average accuracy of different datasets, since the difficulty of different datasets is obviously quite different, which is unreasonable. 

**Response2**:  In addition to the average accuracy (that is the official metric from the DomainBed benchmark), we have now included the ranking information in Tables 3 and 4. The results are the same: Fishr remains the best and most consistent approach by far in the ‘Oracle’ setup, and among the best in the ‘Training’ setup. Moreover, Fishr remains consistently stronger than ERM, which we believe is the main point to validate the effectiveness of our method. Being sometimes lower than another method does not mean Fishr is not efficient, but that the other regularization may be more effective on this task.

**Comment3**: The increase in average accuracy across different datasets is entirely due to the colored MNIST dataset, which happens to be the simplest dataset. 

**Response3**: With all due respect, stating that “the increase in average accuracy across different datasets is entirely due to the colored MNIST dataset” is factually false. In ‘Oracle’, averaging over the 6 other datasets in Table 3 would lead to the following order in average accuracy: 1.Fishr(avg=71.1) 2.CORAL(71.0) 3.Mixup(70.8) 4.ERM(70.5). In other words, even when the Colored MNIST experiment is removed, our approach remains the state of the art on average in ‘Oracle’. Most importantly, though being arguably simple, the Colored MNIST task is the main one to capture correlation shifts (as defined in [1]), and to measure how a method can differentiate causation from correlation. We believe that Fishr performing so well on Colored MNIST is more a strength than a weakness.

[1] Ye, Nanyang, et al. "OoD-Bench: Benchmarking and Understanding Out-of-Distribution Generalization Datasets and Algorithms." arXiv (2021).

replying_to: Replying to Response to reviewer ZMd5 (1/2)

content.title: Response to reviewer ZMd5 (2/2)
content.comment:
**Comment4**: Thirdly, the fair setting(Table 4) does not show any benefits

**Response4**: We strongly disagree with describing the ‘Training-domain model selection’ as “the fair setting”, and this for at least three reasons. 

First, as argued in the “limitations” paragraph from Section 4.2.2, the ‘Training’ setup suffers from *underspecification* [1]. Indeed, selecting the model with the best training accuracy is suboptimal: we cited [2] to suggest that future benchmarks may consider the training calibration instead.

Second, learning *causal* mechanisms can be useless in this ‘Training’ setup. Indeed, when the correlations are more predictive in training than the causal features, the variant model would be selected over the invariant one. This explains the poor results for all methods in ‘Training’ ColoredMNIST (Table 4). As a side note, the best model on ‘Training’ Colored MNIST is ARM that uses test time adaptation - thus in a sense uses information from the test-domain - and whose contribution is mostly complementary to ours.

Third, we believe that the ‘Oracle’ model selection is more *realistic* for real applications. Indeed, one user would easily label some samples to validate the efficiency of its algorithm. It’s not realistic to believe that the user would simply deploy this new algorithm without at least checking that the performances are correct. We recall that the ‘Oracle’ setup in DomainBed benchmark is quite restricting, allowing only one evaluation per choice of hyperparameters.

That’s why [3] even states that “OOD performance cannot, by definition, be performed with a validation set from the same distribution as the training data”. Both opinions being reasonable and arguable, we included Training and Oracle results for the sake of completeness. Even if the improvements are smaller than in Table 3, Fishr remains stronger than ERM in the ‘Training’ setup from Table 4. Yet, our state-of-the-art results on the ‘Oracle’ setup alone are sufficient to prove the usefulness of our approach for real-world applications.

[1] D'Amour, Alexander, et al. "Underspecification presents challenges for credibility in modern machine learning." arXiv (2020).

[2] Wald, Yoav, et al. "On calibration and out-of-domain generalization." arXiv (2021).

[3] Teney, Damien, et al. "Evading the Simplicity Bias: Training a Diverse Set of Models Discovers Solutions with Superior OOD Generalization." arXiv (2021).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a simple technique for out-of-distribution generalization, called Fishr. Intuitively, given the success of CORAL, Fishr enforces consistency through mean regularization between the element-wise variances of the gradients across domains. It is efficiently solvable using the existing BackPACK package. Several explanations have been provided for Fishr. Then, the paper concludes with applying Fishr to standard OOD benchmarks showing superior performance of Fishr in several different problems.
content.main_review:
This paper introduces a simple technique for out-of-distribution generalization, called Fishr. Intuitively, given the success of CORAL, Fishr enforces consistency through mean regularization between the element-wise variances of the gradients in the last layer across domains. It is efficiently solvable using the existing BackPACK package. Several explanations have been provided for Fishr. Then, the paper concludes with applying Fishr to standard OOD benchmarks showing superior performance of Fishr in several different problems.

Overall the algorithm is simple and the idea iand the empirical results are good, which is why I am in support of accepting the paper. However, the presentation of the paper needs major revision to make it more easily followable as suggested below.
- The mathematical exposition of the paper is disjoint from the actual algorithm. For example, the objective in Section 3.1, Eq. (2) is not what is being solved. Please structure the paper to expose the objective being tackled from the beginning. The material on full covariance matrix belong to an appendix on further motivation of the problem, as it is confusing the reader.
- Please explicitly call (3) mean regularization, and refer to it elsewhere as such too, as it is not clear from reading the abstract and intro how the consistency between element-wise variances of the gradients in the last layer is enforced.
- Please restructure Section 3.3.1, and start with the well-known fact that under certain regularity assumptions the Fisher information matrix is proportional to the Hessian of the log loss. Then talk about the caveats of the empirical Fisher information. As is presented now, it is confusing the reader.
- Please give due credit to original work; in several instances recent papers are cited for well-known results dating back several centuries.
- Please bring a condensed version of the pseudo-code to the main paper and ground the discussion of the implementation on it, as it was confusing for me to follow the implementation.
- In several instances, the algorithm refers to Eq. (2)-(4). This is not accurate as those equations capture the covariance of the gradients and not what is being implemented. By changing those equations to capture what is being implemented, this consistency will also be resolved.
- Hyperparameter \gamma is not defined in the implementation section while it is part of Sec 5.2.1 and the pseudo-code. Please move the exposition up to where it belongs.
- The connections in Section A.2 with NTK are loose, but I think it is okay the way it is framed now.

From a technical/theoretical standpoint, this paper is indeed weak. 
- Can you say something about what Fishr does in linear/logistic regression? In this case, the implementation captures the actual element-wise variances of the gradients? Is there a toy example that could be devised to be presented right in the beginning to ground the exposition? Is there simple theory that could be used to justify this choice, at least for linear models?
- There are no convergence guarantees for the proposed algorithm.


Typo:
- Pg 5, Section 3.3.1: an unique -> a unique
- Pg 8, Section 5.2.1: an high -> a high
- Pg. 22, Section C.2.2: |\mathcal{E}| + 1 times -> ( |\mathcal{E}| + 1) times
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the paper provides a simple yet powerful method to address out-of-domain generalization with good empirical results, and hence I am in support of acceptance. However, the paper needs a major rewriting to flesh out the main ideas and make the exposition as straightforward as the proposed algorithm is. Also, the paper lacks theoretical justification for the choice of regularizer and convergence guarantees, which makes it weak from a technical perspective.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper107 by Reviewer Mhdk

content.title: Response to reviewer Mhdk
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer Mhdk. Thank you for your valuable and overall positive comments, notably concerning the theoretical justification.
You proposed several ideas to improve the writing that we very much appreciated: most have been included in the last revision of our paper. The main change is that now the Equations 2-3-4 directly tackle the variance of the gradient, thus resolving the potential inconsistencies. When applying this exact objective on all layers, we obtain even better results (71.2) than previously (69.5) on Colored MNIST in Table 2. This fixes the discrepancy between the theoretical justification and the actual implementation (as explained in the General Response to All Reviewers). To further facilitate the reading, we have restructured Section 3.3.1 as requested. Moreover, we have included the pseudo-code in the main paper at the place where the hyperparameter gamma is defined. We also modified some citations (in particular [1]) and fixed the typos. We hope that following responses can solve your other concerns.

[1] Fisher, Ronald A. "On the mathematical foundations of theoretical statistics." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. (1922).

**Comment1**: Fishr in the linear setting

**Response1**: We previously used Colored MNIST to illustrate the mechanisms behind Fishr regularization, in particular in Section 3.3, in Section 4.1 and in Appendix B.2.
To further prove the Fishr effectiveness in the linear case, we added a *new experiment* following the binary classification dataset proposed in Fish [1]. Each example is composed of 4 features (f1, f2, f3, f4): f1 is invariant across the two training domains, while (f2, f3, f4) are spurious features. While ERM mostly relies on features (f2, f3), we show that the Fishr regularization forces the linear model to rely mostly on f1, achieving the same accuracy of 93% in train and test domains.

| Method | Train acc. | Test acc. | Weights for [f1, f2, f3, f4] |
|--------|------------|-----------|------------------------------|
| ERM    | 97         | 57        | [2.8,3.3,3.3,0.0]            |
| Fish   | 93         | 93        | [0.4,0.2,0.2,0.0]            |
| Fishr  | 93         | 93        | [2.0,1.2,1.2,0.0]            |

This experiment is further detailed in the new Appendix A.3.1 If you think it’s best included in the main paper, we will be glad to update our revision.

Moreover, in the new Appendix A.3.2, we now *theoretically* prove that matching uncentered gradient variance in a linear binary classifier forces domain-level mean squared errors to be similar across domains, as motivated in V-REx [2].
More generally, we show that ​​Fishr matches weighted squared errors, with weighting schemes depending on the feature distributions.
This is more easily understood when features are binary, in {0,1}: in that case, Fishr applies domain-level risks matching on groups of samples having a shared feature. This describes Fishr as an features-adaptive version of V-REx. This further justifies theoretically our gradient variance matching.

[1] Shi, Yuge, et al. "Gradient Matching for Domain Generalization." arXiv (2021).

[2] Krueger, David, et al. "Out-of-distribution generalization via risk extrapolation (rex)." ICML. 2021.

**Comment2**: Convergence guarantees for Fishr
 
**Response2**: If the network is sufficiently parametrized and after enough training steps, the network would perfectly predict all training samples. At that point, the training gradients would be zero, thus so do gradient variances and our penalty. In conclusion, our approach converges as long as the network can fit the training dataset. In practice, best generalization performances are obtained long before convergence, thus motivating early stopping. Note that the number of training steps is fixed to 501 in Colored MNIST and 5000 in DomainBed. Finally, this question is highly related to the comment4 from reviewer KDTu.

**Comment3**: Average performance is misleading

**Response3**: Thank you for suggesting the *ranking information* in DomainBed. We now also report the {arithmetic mean, geometric mean, median, best, worst} ranking of each algorithm. Overall, the analyses are the same when comparing rankings or average accuracies: Fishr remains the best performing approach by far in the ‘Oracle’ setup, and among the best in the ‘Training’ setup.

content.title: Response to reviewer iWJv
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer iWJv, thank you for your feedback and for highlighting our extensive experiments. We will address your concerns below.

**Comment1**: Limited contribution over previous work. The proposed method can be seen as a heuristic extension of gradient alignment (e.g. fish). Proper theoretical justification is in absence.

**Response1**: Fishr introduces an empirical strategy, motivated and justified with arguments from previous theoretical works in Section 3.3, whose insights are systematically empirically validated. Moreover, as referenced in Section 3.3.2, we further theoretically generalize the upper bound of domain inconsistencies in Appendix A.1. Fish [1] and Fishr both tackle gradients and have close names. Except that their theoretical motivations, their implementations and empirical performances are very different.

*Theoretically*, Fish tries to find shared minimas across domains in the loss landscapes by aligning gradient means. In contrast, Fishr is the first method to consider and talk about gradient distributions. This insight could motivate future works to match gradient distributions with adversarial methods. Yet, Fishr is not just a generalization of Fish to higher-order statistics: the main point in Fishr is the domain-level Hessians matching. We notably illustrate the “connection between proposed method and Fisher Information '' in Section 3.3, as you highlighted in your review. This reduces inconsistencies across domains, as shown in Appendix A.1.

The *implementations* are also totally different. Fish leverages a meta-learning algorithm that is arguably impractical because $|\mathcal{E}|$ longer to train than ERM. On the contrary, Fishr “is effectively optimized with faster approximation, which relieves the computational overhead” as you also noticed.

*Empirically*, in our main ‘Oracle’ setup, Fishr performs much better than Fish while being much more efficient; indeed, Fish is consistently worse than ERM on real-world datasets. In conclusion, Fishr is much more useful than Fish for real-world applications, both in terms of scalability and pure performance.

[1] Shi, Yuge, et al. "Gradient Matching for Domain Generalization." arXiv (2021).

**Comment2**: Empirical results are not convincing enough to support the strong claim. The proposed method rarely beats all the baselines (1 out of 14 settings), and the average performance over all the datasets is extremely misleading.

**Response2**: Our main empirical claim is to *improve over ERM*. This is achieved systematically on all setups in DomainBed [1]. Critically, we are the only method to do so. This is because the ERM from DomainBed is “carefully tuned”: notably, this strong baseline “outperform[ed] the previously published state-of-the-art results”. Moreover, Fishr beats ERM despite the restricted hyperparameter search, which penalizes approaches with additional hyperparameters. Indeed, we can only sample 20 configurations of hyperparameters, with the same hyperparameter distributions across the different imposed datasets (see Section C.2.3).

Our second empirical claim is to be *consistently among the best methods*, which we now further highlight by adding the ranking information in Tables 3 and 4. In ‘Oracle’, Fishr is in the top4 for all real-world datasets, with a median ranking of second. No method is always the best: yet, Fishr is the most consistently on the podium. This ranking information validates the average accuracy, arguably partial even if chosen as the official metric of this public benchmark.

Moreover, Fishr is *complementary* to other methods: in Appendix C.2.2, we show that Fishr and IGA can be used together for improved accuracy.

In conclusion, our method performs remarkably well in the open-source DomainBed, which is currently the main and fairer benchmark to compare approaches for out-of-distribution generalization. All our results are easily reproducible. This validates Fishr as a simple and efficient method to be applicable for real-world usages, and thus the significance of our empirical contributions.

[1] Gulrajani, Ishaan, and David Lopez-Paz. "In search of lost domain generalization." ICLR (2021).

content.title: General response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their thoughtful remarks. We have tried to answer your questions individually. Moreover, your feedback enabled us to update a new version of the paper. In addition to some minor improvements (colored citations, clarity in Section 3.3.1, pseudo-code in the main paper), we targeted 2 concerns:
1. We reduce the discrepancy between our theoretical justification and our actual implementation. Contrary to what reviewers iWJv and ZMd5 argue, our work already theoretically justified the gradient covariance matching: via the Fisher information matrix, we show in Section 3.3 and Appendix A.1 that Fishr matches domain-level Hessians and reduces inconsistencies across domains. Yet, we agree with reviewers Mhdk and KDTu that our actual implementation was slightly different due to approximations necessary for computational reasons on DomainBed. To fix this, Equations 2-3 now directly capture the gradient variances. We have also implemented our gradient variance matching in all layers - rather than only applying Fishr in the classifier. In Table 2, this works even better to tackle correlation shifts in Colored MNIST, from 69.5 to 71.2 in test. Finally, in Appendix A.3, we now show and analyze Fishr effectiveness in the linear case.

2. We further demonstrate the empirical significance of our strategy on DomainBed. To do so, we add the ranking information (arithmetic mean, geometric mean, median, best, worst) in Tables 3 and 4 as suggested by reviewer Mhdk: Fishr outperforms all other approaches, with a median ranking of second in our main ‘Oracle’ setup. This ranking validates the average accuracy. We also include a new color formatting to further show “visually” that Fishr is the only method to consistently improve ERM, and to highlight the poor performances of previous gradient-based methods (notably Fish and AND-mask). These performances are significant due to the importance of the DomainBed benchmark in our community: by imposing the datasets, the training procedure and controlling the hyperparameter search, DomainBed is arguably the fairer open-source benchmark.
